x-notifications.name: attach.hello
x-notifications.connection-state: first frame only, before raw terminal bytes
x-notifications.description: attach.sock begins with a frontend-to-daemon attach.hello notification (no id); named and ordered version,rows,cols,terminal positional parameters retain the existing Serde forms. Version 1 and nonzero u16 dimensions are checked after structural decoding; bad version or zero dimensions retain the unsupported-version diagnostic. A supplied terminal requires 1..500 dimensions during target attachment, after the existing state/policy checks. Hello has a 4 KiB body and 3-second frame deadline, eight pending hellos per goblin and at most four accepts per tick. The daemon reads exactly the hello frame and consumes no following raw bytes.

x-notifications.name: attach.waiting
x-notifications.description: While startup or required onAttach variables are pending, the daemon sends attach.waiting with a required missing array, initially/periodically at one-second intervals. Empty missing means startup/draining; nonempty names identify variables that must be fresh and nonempty this run. A live competing attachment refuses without resizing. An exited onAttach client retains its physical stream until the frontend closes; new hellos receive empty waiting notices during that drain.

x-completions.name: attach.reply
x-completions.description: Completion after a valid modern hello and any waiting notifications. Modern attach.sock and legacy terminal.sock complete with a correlated JSON-RPC response of id 0: result attached=true, or error -32009 with a diagnostic. Only success switches the stream to raw bytes. terminal.sock is server-first with no hello; it retains stopped output, waits for configuration/readiness and refuses onAttach goblins with an upgrade message. Modern named-terminal attachments answer at once without waiting notices and redraw before live output. The generic runtime Terminal::attach retains its private caller-supplied id (including nonzero test ids); public entrypoints pass 0. Byte queues, refusal-before-resize, descriptor ownership, cancellation and framed/raw boundaries remain handwritten.
